title: Please… Enough with the Sloppy, One-Shot SaaS Replacements — Mahmoud Abdelwahab, Railway
talk_summary: Mahmoud Abdelwahab describes building Railway's internal all-in-one marketing/CRM/content tool entirely with agents, and lists the product-experience patterns agents skip unless explicitly prompted (autosave, optimistic updates, undo, archiving, URL state, infinite scroll). His core mechanism claims are: give agents a well-abstracted codebase to copy patterns from, package opinions as agent skills, and always close with an end-to-end verification loop where the agent runs the app and fixes what fails.

takeaways.what_they_do: Instead of trusting 'build passed, tests pass', he requires the agent to actually run the feature against real infrastructure, observe failure, and iterate until it works end to end.
takeaways.evidence_quote: you should verify that the feature works end to end and use it by actually running infrastructure and to test things end to end

takeaways.what_they_do: Recurring opinions (UI/typography/error messages, animations, deploy platform usage) are written once as skills the agent loads, rather than re-specified per task.
takeaways.evidence_quote: whenever you have opinions about something they should be packaged as agent skills

takeaways.technique: Reference existing pages/code as canonical examples
takeaways.what_they_do: Explicitly tells the agent to use an existing, good implementation as the reference for UI, data fetching, and structure, so new features copy established patterns instead of inventing new ones.
takeaways.evidence_quote: telling the agent explicitly to use existing pages as references when it comes to the UI the data fetching

takeaways.what_they_do: Maintains a named list of UX patterns agents omit by default (autosave, optimistic updates, undo, archive, URL state, infinite scroll) and asks for them explicitly, sometimes via a planning pass.
takeaways.evidence_quote: there are kind of like a bunch of patterns that I found that agents don't typically do unless you explicitly ask them to

takeaways.technique: Solid abstractions to stop agents reinventing patterns
takeaways.what_they_do: Argues language/framework matters less than a well-structured codebase with solid abstractions, because agents then follow existing patterns instead of introducing new ones per feature.
takeaways.evidence_quote: the agent doesn't need to reinvent the same like wheel every time it tries to add a new feature

takeaways.what_they_do: Notes the gap between one-shotted working software and polished software, and jokes about token burn for ambitious features (real-time collab).
takeaways.evidence_quote: just 700 million tokens later, I had real time
takeaways.numbers: ~700M tokens for one real-time collaboration feature
